title: Slowed Rossby Wave Phase Speed Over Siberia Linking Arctic Warm Conditions to Mid‐Latitude Cold Anomalies
content:
Abstract

The influence of Arctic warming on mid-latitude cold extremes remains a subject of active debate, with the role of Rossby wave propagation emerging as a key aspect warranting investigation. Here, we examine wintertime Rossby wave phase speed changes over Siberia and their relationship with Arctic warm conditions on intraseasonal timescales. We identify a significant slowdown of Rossby wave phase speed over Siberia in recent decades, and show that Arctic warm winters are associated with low phase speeds in this region. The reduced phase speed corresponds to a westward shift of anti-cyclonic circulation over eastern Siberia, favoring the persistence of cold anomalies over Eurasia. Cluster analysis reveals that this westward-shifting pattern has occurred more frequently during Arctic warm spells since the 2000s, enhancing the co-occurrence of Arctic warming and cold anomalies over Eurasia and North America. Model simulations further indicate that the slowdown of phase speed over Siberia is closely linked to Arctic sea ice loss and reproduces the observed close relationship between low phase speed and continental cold temperatures, especially for Eurasia. These findings suggest that slower Rossby wave phase speed over Siberia serves as a link between Arctic warming and mid-latitude cooling.
